objetivo.en: Say what you want to do and what you can do with querer + infinitive and poder + infinitive, and offer help.

nota.en: quiero, quieres, quiere… (e becomes ie, except nosotros).
puedo, puedes, puede… (o becomes ue, except nosotros).

explicacion.en: After quiero or puedo, the second verb stays in the infinitive (llevar, comprar, cocinar). Only the first verb changes with the person.
English “I want to buy” has a “to”, but Spanish does not add any word: quiero + infinitive.
Only the second verb stays in the infinitive. The first verb must change with the person: yo quiero, not “yo querer”.
The second verb is never conjugated: quiere comprar, not quiere compra.
After puedo, use the infinitive pagar, not the yo form pago.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the soft d

texto.en: Between two vowels, the Spanish d is soft: it sounds like the “th” in “this”, but lighter, with the tongue barely touching the teeth. Say it in puedo, todo, nada and comida. At the beginning of a word, or after n or l, the d is firmer, like an English d: don Jorge, dólares. Say them slowly: puedo, puedes, podemos, todo.

To say what you want to do, use querer + infinitive: Quiero comprar tomates. To say what you can do, or to ask permission or offer help, use poder + infinitive: Puedo llevar las bolsas. ¿Puedo ayudar? The first verb is conjugated in the present and the second verb always stays in the infinitive (comprar, llevar, cocinar). Spanish adds no word for the English “to”: quiero comprar is “I want to buy”. Both verbs are stem-changing, as you saw before: querer becomes quiero, quieres, quiere, quieren (e to ie) and poder becomes puedo, puedes, puede, pueden (o to ue). Only nosotros keeps the plain stem: queremos, podemos. For no, put no before the first verb: No quiero cocinar hoy. No puedo venir el sábado. Use ¿quieres…? to invite a friend or someone younger (tú), and ¿Puedo pagar con tarjeta? to ask if you can pay by card. Emma uses usted with señora Rosa, and señora Rosa uses tú with Emma.

titulo.en: I have to peel the onion

objetivo.en: Say what you have to do and what one has to do in the kitchen, and tell what you do with hago, pongo, salgo and traigo.

nota.en: yo hago. The h is silent.
yo pongo. Poner la mesa = to set the table.
In Latin America, papa is the potato.

explicacion.en: To say “I have to”, Spanish needs que: tengo que + infinitive. Without que, tengo means only “I have”.
Hay que is for everyone and never changes. It is always followed by the infinitive: hay que pelar.
Hace is for él, ella and usted. With yo, use the -go form: hago. Only yo is irregular; tú haces, ella hace.
The little word que is required: hay que + infinitive.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the g

texto.en: Before a, o and u, the Spanish g is a hard g like the g in “go”: hago, pongo, salgo, traigo. Before e and i it sounds like a strong h (like the Spanish j): gente. Note that in hago the h is silent, so it sounds like “AH-goh”. Say them slowly: hago, pongo, salgo, traigo.

titulo.en: Tener que, hay que and the -go verbs

texto.en: To say what you have to do, use tener que + infinitive: Tengo que lavar las papas. Tienes que pelar la cebolla. You need que: English “I have to wash” is tengo que lavar. To say what has to be done by anyone, or by everyone, use hay que + infinitive: Hay que lavar las frutas. Hay que never changes, so it works like “one has to” or “you have to” in general. Four very common verbs end in -go in the yo form: hacer becomes hago, poner becomes pongo, salir becomes salgo, and traer becomes traigo. All the other persons are regular: haces, pones, sales, traes. Tener is also a -go verb: tengo. Use them to say what you do: Hago la sopa. Pongo la mesa. Traigo el arroz. Salgo a las siete. Combine them with the structures you know: Tengo que hacer la sopa. Quiero salir a las siete. Emma talks to señora Rosa with usted and Rosa answers with tú.
Only the yo form is irregular. Tap each form to hear it.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: the silent h

texto.en: In Spanish, the letter h is always silent. You never pronounce it: huevos sounds like “WEH-vohs”, harina like “ah-REE-nah”, hoy like “oy”. Be careful: ch is a different sound, like the ch in “chair”. Say them slowly: huevos, harina, hoy, hola.

To ask for food at the market, say the quantity or the container, then de, then the food: una libra de tomates (a pound of tomatoes), medio kilo de queso (half a kilo of cheese), un kilo de arroz, un litro de leche, una botella de aceite (a bottle of oil), un paquete de harina (a package of flour). There is no article after de. Un poco de means “a little”: un poco de sal. Mucho, mucha, muchos and muchas mean “a lot of” and agree with the noun: mucha leche, muchos huevos, mucho queso, muchas frutas. To order politely, you know quisiera: Quisiera una libra de tomates. With usted, you can also ask ¿Me da medio kilo de queso? (Can you give me half a kilo of cheese?). The market in Ecuador often sells by the libra, while cheese and rice come by the kilo. Add por favor at the end: Una botella de aceite, por favor.
Mucho agrees in gender and number with the noun that follows.

nota.en: A man is el cajero. The j is a strong h.

explicacion.en: Use cien only for exactly 100. Before another number it becomes ciento: ciento cuarenta y cinco.

English says “one thousand”, but Spanish uses mil without un: mil dólares.
Put y only between the tens and the units. There is no y after the hundreds.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: c, z and s

texto.en: In Latin American Spanish, the letter s, the letter z and c before e or i all sound the same, like the “s” in “see”. There is no “th” sound. So cien, ciento, doscientos and quinientos all use a clear “s” sound, and so do arroz and almuerzo. Say them slowly: cien, ciento, doscientos, quinientos.

The number 100 is cien when it stands alone: cien dólares. Before another number it becomes ciento: ciento veinte (120), ciento cuarenta y cinco (145). The other hundreds are doscientos (200), trescientos (300), cuatrocientos (400), quinientos (500), seiscientos (600), setecientos (700), ochocientos (800) and novecientos (900). Watch the irregular spellings: quinientos, setecientos and novecientos. 1000 is mil, never un mil. From 200 to 900, the hundreds agree in gender with the noun: doscientos dólares, but doscientas libras. Cien, ciento and mil do not change. To build a compound number, say the hundreds first, then the tens, then y, then the units: trescientos cuarenta y cinco (345). Do not put y after the hundreds: ciento veinte, not “ciento y veinte”. In Ecuador, prices are in dollars: ¿Cuánto cuesta? Cuesta quinientos dólares.
Tap each number to hear it.

objetivo.en: Answer without repeating the noun, using lo, la, los or las, when something is offered to you while shopping.

traduccion.en: it / him (replaces a masculine singular noun)
it / her (replaces a feminine singular noun)

explicacion.en: In English “it” and “them” go after the verb, but in Spanish lo, la, los and las go before the conjugated verb: lo quiero.
The pronoun agrees with the noun it replaces. If you are talking about las naranjas (feminine plural), use las.
Do not use lo for everything. Leche is feminine, so the pronoun is la: la quiero.

titulo.en: Sound of the day: r and rr

texto.en: The letter r is called erre. At the beginning of a word, and in rr, the Spanish r is strong: the tongue taps several times against the roof of the mouth, a trill. Say arroz (spelled with rr), rico, rojo, carro, perro with a strong r. A single r between two vowels is soft: one quick tap, like the “tt” in American English “butter”: para, pero, naranja, cero. Do not confuse them: pero (but) has a soft r, and perro (dog) has a trill.

titulo.en: Lo, la, los, las: answering without repeating the noun

texto.en: When someone offers you something, you do not need to repeat the noun. Use lo, la, los or las instead, as English uses “it” and “them”: ¿Quiere el queso? Sí, lo quiero. The pronoun agrees with the noun it replaces: el aguacate becomes lo, la leche becomes la, los tomates becomes los and las naranjas becomes las. Careful: the pronoun la is the same word as the article la, but it goes right before the conjugated verb. Unlike English, the pronoun goes before the verb: lo quiero, las compro, los llevo, not “quiero lo”. In a negative answer, no goes first: No, no lo quiero. No, no las llevo. Here the vendor uses usted: ¿Lleva las manzanas? You answer: Sí, las llevo. or No, no las llevo.
The pronoun matches the gender and number of the noun. Tap each phrase to hear it.

consigna.en: Choose the pronoun: “Do you want the cheese? — Yes, I want it.”

feedback.en: El queso is masculine singular, so the pronoun is lo.

consigna.en: Complete: “Do you want the oranges? — Yes, I want them.”

feedback.en: Las naranjas is feminine plural, so the pronoun is las.

consigna.en: Match each noun with its pronoun.

feedback.en: El aguacate: lo. La manzana: la. Los tomates: los. Las naranjas: las.

consigna.en: Complete: “Do you take the milk? — No, I don't take it.”

feedback.en: La leche is feminine singular: no la llevo.

consigna.en: Listen and choose what she is talking about.

feedback.en: Las refers to a feminine plural noun: las naranjas.

consigna.en: Put in order: “Yes, I want it.” (the cheese)

feedback.en: Sí, lo quiero. The pronoun goes before the verb.

consigna.en: The seller asks if you want the cheese. Write in Spanish: “No, I don't want it.”

feedback.en: No, no lo quiero. The first no is the answer; the second no goes before the pronoun.

consigna.en: The seller asks about las naranjas. Choose your answer: “Yes, I buy them.”

feedback.en: Las naranjas is feminine plural: las.

contexto.en: At the market, the vendor offers Emma three things. Emma and the vendor use usted with each other.

dialogo.texto: Buenos días, señora. ¿Lleva el aguacate?

traduccion.en: Good morning, ma'am. Are you taking the avocado?

dialogo.texto: Sí, lo llevo.
¿Y las naranjas? ¿Las lleva?

traduccion.en: And the oranges? Are you taking them?

dialogo.texto: No, no las llevo, gracias.

traduccion.en: No, I'm not taking them, thanks.

dialogo.texto: ¿Y las manzanas? Son muy buenas.

traduccion.en: And the apples? They are very good.

dialogo.texto: Sí, las llevo.

consigna.en: Does Emma take the avocado?

feedback.en: Emma says Sí, lo llevo: she takes it.

consigna.en: Does Emma take the oranges?

feedback.en: Emma says No, no las llevo: she doesn't take them.

consigna.en: The seller asks about la leche. Choose your answer: “Yes, I take it.”

feedback.en: La leche is feminine singular: la.

consigna.en: Complete: “The tomatoes? Yes, I buy them.”

feedback.en: Los tomates is masculine plural: los.

consigna.en: Listen and choose the meaning.

feedback.en: Los refers to a masculine plural noun, and no means no.

consigna.en: Put in order: “Yes, I buy them.” (los tomates)

feedback.en: Sí, los compro.

consigna.en: The seller asks if you take the avocado. Write in Spanish: “Yes, I take it.”

feedback.en: Sí, lo llevo. El aguacate is masculine: lo.

consigna.en: The seller asks if you take the apples. Write in Spanish: “Yes, I take them.”

feedback.en: Sí, las llevo. Las manzanas is feminine plural: las.
